title: Uniform Resource Locators (URL)
summary: Specifies the Uniform Resource Locator (URL), the syntax and semantics of formalized strings that name the location and access method for resources on the Internet. It is on the standards track. It has been replaced by later documents, including RFC 4248 and RFC 4266.

eli5.summary: The web address you type, which tells your computer where something is and how to get it.

questions: what characters must be encoded in a url
what are the default ports for url schemes
subtitle: The original definition of the URL: a compact string that says where a resource is and how to reach it.

tldr.problem: The Internet had many ways to reach resources (FTP, HTTP, Gopher, mail, news and more) but no common, compact way to write down where something is and how to get it.
tldr.mechanism: A URL is written as a scheme, a colon and a scheme-specific part. A shared syntax covers user, password, host, port and path, and the RFC defines schemes such as ftp, http, gopher, mailto, news, nntp, telnet, wais, file and prospero.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1738 is obsoleted by RFC 4248 and RFC 4266 per the metadata, and has been updated by several later RFCs, so it is no longer the current definition.

today: RFC 1738 is obsoleted by RFC 4248 and RFC 4266, and has been updated by RFC 1808, RFC 2368, RFC 2396, RFC 3986, RFC 6196, RFC 6270 and RFC 8089. Read those for current rules.

sections.title: What a URL Is
sections.content:
RFC 1738 specifies the Uniform Resource Locator (URL), a compact string representation for a resource available via the Internet. It builds on concepts from the World-Wide Web initiative, whose use of such objects dates from 1990, and was written by the URI working group of the IETF.

URLs locate resources by giving an abstract identification of the location. Once located, a system might access, update, replace or find attributes of the resource, but in general only the access method needs to be specified for a scheme. A URL is written <scheme>:<scheme-specific-part>. Scheme names may use lowercase letters, digits, plus, period and hyphen, and programs should treat uppercase as equivalent to lowercase.
sections.eli5: A URL starts with a word saying how to fetch something, then a colon, then the details of where it is.

sections.title: Characters and Percent Encoding
sections.content:
URLs are written with the printable US-ASCII characters. Any octet can be written as % followed by two hexadecimal digits. Octets MUST be encoded if they have no graphic US-ASCII character (the octets 00-1F, 7F and 80-FF), if the character is unsafe, or if it is reserved for another meaning in the scheme.

Unsafe characters include the space, <, >, the quote mark, the number sign (which delimits a fragment), %, and { } | \ ^ ~ [ ] and the backquote. Characters that may be reserved for special meaning in a scheme are ; / ? : @ = &. Only alphanumerics, the special characters $-_.+!*'(),, and reserved characters used for their reserved purpose may appear unencoded.
sections.eli5: Some characters have special jobs or get mangled in transit, so they are written as a percent sign and two digits, like putting a tricky word in a safe code.

sections.title: Common Internet Scheme Syntax
sections.content:
Schemes that use an IP-based protocol to a host share one form: //<user>:<password>@<host>:<port>/<url-path>. The user, password, port and path parts can each be left out. A password cannot be given without a user name, and an empty user name differs from none at all.

The host is a fully qualified domain name or an IP address as four decimal groups. The rightmost domain label never starts with a digit, which tells names apart from addresses. The port is decimal, and most schemes have a default. The / before the url-path is not part of the path. A scheme may be hierarchical, with / separating components, as in ftp, http and file. The RFC does not describe relative links.
sections.eli5: Many addresses follow one pattern: who you are, which computer, which door on it, and which shelf to look at. You can skip any part you do not need.

sections.title: The Defined Schemes
sections.content:
Section 3 defines ten schemes. ftp (default port 21) turns the path into CWD commands followed by a transfer, with an optional ;type= of a, i or d, and anonymous FTP conventions apply when no login is given. http (port 80) is http://<host>:<port>/<path>?<searchpart> and allows no user name or password. gopher (port 70) carries a type character, selector, optional search and Gopher+ string.

mailto holds an RFC 822 address and designates no data object. news names a group or a message ID and is location-independent, while nntp (port 119) names a group and article on one server, and the news form is preferred. telnet (port 23) designates an interactive service, with user and password advisory only. wais (port 210) names a database, search or document. file names a file on a host, with localhost or empty meaning the local machine. prospero (port 1525) uses a host-specific object name.
sections.eli5: Each scheme is a different delivery service: one for file servers, one for web pages, one for mail addresses, one for discussion groups, and so on. Each says how to write its addresses.

sections.title: New Schemes and Security
sections.content:
New schemes are introduced by defining a mapping onto the conforming syntax with a new prefix. IANA maintains a registry of URL schemes, and a submission must define an access algorithm and syntax and show demonstrable utility and operability. Scheme names starting with x- are reserved for experimental use. Names proposed but left undefined include afs, mid, cid, nfs, tn3270, mailserver and z39.50.

The security section says the URL scheme itself poses no threat, but a URL does not guarantee it will keep pointing to the same object. A crafted URL with a non-default port can make a client send protocol commands to a server of a different protocol, and the RFC cites gopher URLs used to send a rude message through an SMTP server. Encoded delimiters such as CR and LF should not be decoded before transmission, and putting secret passwords in URLs is unwise.
sections.eli5: New address types need to be registered and shown to work. And be careful: a tricky address can send the wrong kind of message to the wrong kind of computer, so never put secrets in one.
